text: How much E. coli data is there — expression studies and raw sequencing runs?

## Abstract  
We quantified publicly available Escherichia coli (E. coli) high-throughput data in two categories that underpin many systems-biology and genomics analyses: (i) raw sequencing runs and (ii) processed gene-expression studies. Using NCBI’s Sequence Read Archive (SRA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) via programmatic queries, we found 631 325 individual SRA runs and 1 929 GEO Series (GSE) records annotated with the organism term “Escherichia coli”. These numbers, retrieved on 17 September 2026, provide an updated baseline of the volume of E. coli data. The roughly 3 000-fold excess of raw sequencing runs over curated expression studies highlights the continued dominance of primary sequencing in prokaryotic genomics and the comparatively modest deposition of processed expression datasets. These figures inform resource planning for large-scale meta-analyses and benchmarking efforts in microbial genomics.

## I. Introduction  
Background.  Escherichia coli is a model bacterium and a major pathogen. Public omics repositories capture its genetic diversity (raw sequencing) and transcriptional responses (expression profiling), both of which are essential for comparative genomics, antimicrobial-resistance surveillance, and systems-biology modelling.  
Literature Review.  No literature was retrieved for this query.  
Knowledge Gap.  The current magnitude of E. coli data in SRA and GEO had not been quantified side-by-side within a single, reproducible analysis.  
Objective & Hypothesis.  We aimed to determine the total counts of (a) raw sequencing runs and (b) expression studies for E. coli in NCBI’s principal archives. We hypothesised that raw sequencing runs would vastly outnumber curated expression studies.

## II. Materials and Methods  
Study Design.  Two targeted database queries were executed: one against SRA for raw runs and one against GEO for expression Series. Tools were chosen for their ability to return total counts without bulk data transfer.  
Materials.  
• NCBI SRA via ncbi_sra_search  
• NCBI GEO via geo_search  

Procedures.  
1. ncbi_sra_search  
   • Arguments: organism="Escherichia coli"; max_results=1 (to minimise payload).  
   • The tool internally executed esearch (retmax = 0) to obtain the total hit count and confirmed it with esummary for one record.  
2. geo_search  
   • Arguments: organism="Escherichia coli"; entry_type="gse" (Series); max_results=1.  
   • The search term was automatically built as `"Escherichia coli"[Organism] AND "gse"[Filter]`.  

Statistical Analysis.  
• Raw counts were taken from:  
  – `result_count` field (SRA) = 631 325.  
  – `total_count` field (GEO) = 1 929.  
• Proportion of expression studies = 1 929 / 633 254 × 100 ≈ 0.31 %.  
• Fold-difference (runs ÷ Series) = 631 325 / 1 929 ≈ 327.  

## III. Results  
Table 1. Public E. coli omics records in NCBI repositories (17 Sep 2026).

| Data category | Repository | Total records | Query date |
|---------------|------------|--------------:|------------|
| Raw sequencing runs | SRA | 631 325 | 2026-09-17 |
| Expression Series (GSE) | GEO | 1 929 | 2026-09-17 |

Findings.  SRA lists 631 325 E. coli sequencing runs. GEO holds 1 929 E. coli Series. Expression studies represent ~0.31 % of the combined 633 254 records. There are ~327 raw runs for every curated expression Series.

## IV. Discussion  
Interpretation.  The data confirm the hypothesis: raw sequencing runs vastly exceed processed expression studies for E. coli.  
Context.  The imbalance reflects lower barriers to depositing primary reads and the relative complexity of generating and submitting processed expression matrices to GEO.  
Limitations.  1) SRA and GEO counts depend on submitter annotations; mis-annotation could under- or over-estimate true numbers. 2) Other repositories (e.g., ENA mirrored runs, ArrayExpress expression sets) were not queried and may add additional records.  
Conclusion & Future Directions.  Researchers leveraging public E. coli data have access to over 600 000 raw sequencing runs but fewer than 2 000 curated expression studies. Future work should extend coverage to additional repositories, assess data quality, and track growth trends over time.

## References  
[1] NCBI SRA. esearch/esummary query for “Escherichia coli” (17 Sep 2026). https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?term=%22Escherichia+coli%22%5BORGN%5D&retmax=0&retmode=json&db=sra  
[2] NCBI GEO. esearch query for “Escherichia coli” AND gse filter (17 Sep 2026). https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Escherichia+coli%22%5BOrganism%5D+AND+%22gse%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  

## Acknowledgments  
We thank the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) for maintaining the SRA and GEO repositories and for providing programmatic access through the E-utilities API.
